chapter: Chemical Reactions and Equations (Class 10 Science, CBSE)
note: Authored MCQs, 40 per concept, 14 Easy / 13 Medium / 13 Hard off the closed Bloom+DOK ladder. Every distractor carries the misconception it reveals, which is what makes a wrong answer diagnostic rather than merely wrong.

2723.stem: Which of the following is an observation that tells us a chemical reaction has taken place?
2723.explanation: Evolution of a gas is one of the five standard indicators of a chemical change, along with change in colour, change in state, change in temperature and formation of a precipitate.

options.why: Stirring is something we do to the mixture, not something the mixture does; it is not evidence of any change.

options.text: The beaker is made of glass
options.why: Confuses a property of the apparatus with a property of the reaction.
Powdering only changes particle size, which is a physical change that speeds a reaction up rather than showing one happened.

2723.stem: A white insoluble solid separating out when two clear solutions are mixed is called
2723.explanation: An insoluble solid formed in a reaction between two solutions is a precipitate, and its appearance is a clear sign of chemical change.

options.why: A solute dissolves in the solvent; a precipitate is what comes out of solution.
The solvent is the dissolving liquid, not the solid that separates.
A residue is what is left on a filter paper after filtering, which is a later step, not the sign itself.

2723.stem: Which change is observed when a magnesium ribbon burns in air?
2723.explanation: Magnesium burns with a dazzling white flame and leaves a white powder of magnesium oxide, so both light and a new substance are seen.

options.text: A dazzling white flame and a white ash
A pale blue flame and a black ash
options.why: Describes the burning of a carbon compound, not of magnesium.
Magnesium is highly reactive in air; assuming nothing happens ignores the reaction entirely.

options.text: A green flame and a brown ash
options.why: Green flames belong to copper salts; the colour of a flame is element-specific.

2723.stem: The souring of milk left outside the refrigerator is an example of
2723.explanation: Souring produces lactic acid, a new substance with a new taste and smell, and the change cannot be reversed, so it is a chemical change.

options.why: A physical change makes no new substance; soured milk cannot be turned back into fresh milk.
The milk stays a liquid throughout, so no change of state has occurred.
Nuclear changes alter the nucleus of an atom and release enormous energy, which is not what happens here.

2723.stem: Which of these is NOT by itself proof that a chemical reaction has occurred?
2723.explanation: Melting is a change of state only: the substance is the same before and after, so melting alone proves nothing about a chemical change.

options.why: A precipitate is a new insoluble substance, which is evidence of a chemical change.
A gas given off is a new substance appearing, which is evidence of a chemical change.
A colour change signals a new substance with different properties has formed.

2723.stem: When dilute hydrochloric acid is added to zinc granules, the observation is
2723.explanation: Zinc lies above hydrogen in the reactivity series, so it displaces hydrogen and brisk effervescence of hydrogen gas is seen.

options.why: Blue solutions come from copper salts; zinc salts are colourless.
Zinc chloride is soluble, so nothing separates out as a solid.
Assumes zinc is unreactive; in fact it is above hydrogen in the reactivity series.

2723.stem: A rise in temperature of the mixture during a reaction shows that the reaction is
2723.explanation: Heat released to the surroundings raises the temperature of the mixture, which is the definition of an exothermic reaction.

options.why: Reverses the definition: an endothermic reaction absorbs heat, so the mixture becomes cooler.
Photochemical describes what starts a reaction (light), not the heat it releases.
Reversibility is about direction, and tells us nothing about heat.

2723.stem: Which observation is seen when carbon dioxide is passed through lime water?
2723.explanation: Insoluble calcium carbonate forms and stays suspended, so the clear lime water turns milky. This is the standard test for carbon dioxide.

options.why: Blue is the colour of copper sulphate solution, not of any product here.
Carbon dioxide puts fires out; it does not burn.
Freezing is a change of state caused by cooling, not by passing a gas through.

2723.stem: Burning of a candle involves
2723.explanation: Wax melts (physical) and the molten wax vapour burns to give carbon dioxide and water (chemical), so both kinds of change happen together.

options.text: both a physical and a chemical change

options.why: Ignores the burning itself, which forms carbon dioxide and water.
Ignores the melting of the wax, which is a change of state.
Something is clearly happening: the candle shortens and gives out heat and light.

2723.stem: The five common indications of a chemical reaction include all of the following EXCEPT
2723.explanation: Change in shape is purely physical; breaking or moulding a substance leaves it chemically the same.

options.why: A new colour means a substance with new properties has formed.
Heat taken in or given out accompanies the making and breaking of bonds.
A gas bubbling off is a new substance appearing.

2723.stem: Rusting of an iron nail left in damp air is recognised by
2723.explanation: Rust is hydrated iron(III) oxide, seen as a reddish-brown flaky coating on the surface of the iron.

options.why: Describes the clean metal before rusting, not the product.
Black coatings form on silver and on copper, not on iron in damp air.
Green coatings form on copper exposed to moist air, not on iron.

2723.stem: Which of the following pairs gives a change in state as the only observation?
2723.explanation: Ice becoming water is melting: the same substance in a different state, with no new substance formed.

options.why: Curdling produces lactic acid, a new substance, so it is a chemical change.
Rust is a new compound with completely different properties from iron.
Burning forms ash and gases that cannot be turned back into wood.

2723.stem: Bubbles seen when an antacid tablet is dropped into water are evidence of
2723.explanation: The tablet's carbonate reacts with its acid ingredient in water to release carbon dioxide, and a gas being produced is a sign of chemical change.

options.why: Boiling needs heating to 100 degrees Celsius; the water here stays cool.
Simple dissolving releases no gas; sugar in water produces no bubbles.
Air already dissolved in water does not come out in a steady stream like this.

2723.stem: A change in which no new substance is formed is called
2723.explanation: A physical change alters only form, state or appearance; the substance itself is unchanged and the change is usually reversible.

options.why: A chemical change is defined precisely by the formation of new substances.
A combination reaction is a type of chemical change, so new substances do form.
Decomposition splits a compound into new, simpler substances.

2723.stem: A student adds a colourless solution to another colourless solution and a bright yellow solid appears. The best conclusion is that
2723.explanation: A new insoluble substance with a new colour has appeared, which is a precipitation reaction, and precipitation is always a chemical change.

options.text: a chemical reaction has formed a new insoluble substance
one solution simply dissolved in the other
options.why: Dissolving gives a clear solution, not a solid that settles out.

options.text: the yellow solid was already present but unseen
options.why: Both solutions were clear, so no solid could have been suspended in them.

options.text: the solutions changed state on mixing
options.why: Both were liquid before and after; a solid appearing is a new substance, not a state change.

2723.stem: Copper sulphate solution turns pale green and a reddish deposit appears on an iron nail dipped in it. The observation showing chemical change is
2723.explanation: Both the colour change of the solution and the new reddish deposit of copper show that new substances have formed.

options.text: the colour change together with the new deposit

options.why: Wetting is just contact with liquid and involves no new substance.

options.text: only the solution being blue at the start
options.why: The starting colour is a property, not a change.

options.text: only the nail being made of iron
options.why: Names a reactant rather than describing any observation.

2723.stem: Quick lime is added to water in a beaker and the beaker becomes hot. This shows that
2723.explanation: Heat given out to the surroundings during the slaking of lime makes this an exothermic chemical reaction.

options.text: an exothermic reaction is taking place
the water is simply being warmed
options.why: No heat was supplied from outside, so the heat must come from the reaction.
Simple dissolving of most solids causes little or no heating, and lime forms a new compound.

options.text: the beaker is a poor conductor
options.why: The beaker's conductivity affects how fast heat spreads, not where it came from.

2723.stem: On heating, a green powder turns black and a gas with a choking smell is released. The number of indications of chemical change present is
2723.explanation: Two indications are present: a change in colour from green to black, and evolution of a gas with a distinctive smell.

options.why: Counts only one of the two distinct observations described.
No change of state or precipitate is mentioned, so only two signs are present.
Both a colour change and a new gas are described explicitly.

2723.stem: A student claims that dissolving common salt in water is a chemical change because the salt disappears. The claim is
2723.explanation: The salt can be recovered unchanged by evaporating the water, so no new substance was formed and the change is physical.

options.text: wrong, because the salt can be recovered unchanged
right, because the salt is no longer visible
options.why: Invisibility is not the test; the test is whether a new substance formed.

options.text: right, because the solution conducts electricity
options.why: Conduction shows ions separating, which happens on dissolving and is still physical.

options.text: wrong, because no water was used up
options.why: Reaches the right conclusion by the wrong reason; water is not consumed in many chemical changes either.

2723.stem: Which pair of observations would most strongly suggest a chemical reaction rather than a physical change?
2723.explanation: A permanent colour change together with a gas being given off cannot be explained by any change of state or dissolving.

options.text: Permanent colour change and gas evolution
Change of shape and change of size
options.why: Both describe the same lump of matter rearranged, with no new substance.
Both are reversible physical processes.
Both only bring substances into closer contact.

2723.stem: Silver chloride kept in sunlight turns from white to grey. The observation indicating chemical change is
2723.explanation: The colour change from white to grey is caused by finely divided silver being set free as the compound decomposes in light.

options.text: the change of colour on exposure to light

options.why: Remaining dry is not a change and so is not evidence of anything.
The physical form is the same before and after.
Describes the container, which allows the change but is not the observation.

2723.stem: Two test tubes both feel cold during a reaction. This tells you that in both
2723.explanation: Heat is being absorbed from the surroundings, including from the glass and your hand, so both reactions are endothermic.

options.text: heat is being absorbed from the surroundings
heat is being released to the surroundings
options.why: Released heat would make the tubes feel warm, not cold.
The temperature change itself proves energy is moving.
A stopped reaction would show no further temperature change at all.

2723.stem: Which of these everyday observations is caused by a chemical change?
2723.explanation: A cut apple browning is oxidation of compounds in the fruit by air, producing new brown substances.

options.text: A cut apple turning brown in air
Water vapour condensing on a cold glass
options.why: Condensation is a change of state; the water is chemically unchanged.

options.text: Salt crystals forming as brine evaporates
options.why: Crystallisation recovers the original salt, so no new substance forms.
The gas inside simply occupies more volume at higher temperature.

2723.stem: A reaction mixture bubbles and its temperature drops at the same time. The observations present are
2723.explanation: A gas is being evolved and heat is being absorbed, so the reaction is both gas-producing and endothermic.

options.text: gas evolution and an endothermic change
gas evolution and an exothermic change
options.why: An exothermic change would raise the temperature, not lower it.
Bubbles are a gas, not a solid settling out of solution.
Bubbling and cooling together cannot be explained by a state change alone.

2723.stem: In an experiment, iron filings and sulphur powder are mixed and the mixture is heated until it glows. The glow indicates
2723.explanation: The glow shows heat and light being released as iron and sulphur combine to form iron sulphide, a new compound.

options.text: energy being released as a new compound forms

options.why: Iron melts near 1538 degrees Celsius, far above the temperature of a school burner.
Evaporation would produce a vapour and leave the iron behind unchanged.
A compound has formed, and its parts can no longer be separated with a magnet.

2723.stem: Which observation would make you doubt that a chemical reaction had occurred?
2723.explanation: If the starting substances can be recovered completely and unchanged, then no new substance was ever formed.

options.text: The starting substances can be recovered unchanged
A gas with a new smell is given off
options.why: A new smell means a substance with new properties has appeared.
A temperature change accompanies the breaking and making of bonds.

options.text: A solid settles at the bottom of the tube
options.why: An insoluble solid forming from two solutions is a precipitate.

2723.stem: A colourless gas that turns lime water milky is bubbled out of a reaction. The gas is most likely
2723.explanation: Turning lime water milky is the characteristic test for carbon dioxide, because insoluble calcium carbonate forms.

options.why: Hydrogen burns with a pop and has no effect on lime water.
Oxygen rekindles a glowing splint but leaves lime water clear.
Nitrogen is unreactive and gives no positive result in any of these tests.

2723.stem: A student mixes two solutions, sees no colour change, no gas and no precipitate, but the tube becomes warm. The student concludes no reaction occurred. This conclusion is
2723.explanation: A temperature change is itself one of the recognised indications of a chemical reaction, so the evidence does point to a reaction even though the other four signs are absent.

options.text: unjustified, because a temperature change is itself evidence
justified, because three of the signs are missing
options.why: Treats the indicators as a checklist needing a majority; any single one is sufficient evidence.
Equates chemical change with visible change; neutralisation is invisible yet certainly chemical.

options.text: unjustified, because the tube was made of glass
options.why: Reaches the right verdict for an irrelevant reason.

2723.stem: Burning of magnesium and rusting of iron are both oxidation reactions, yet only one shows a flame. The best explanation is that
2723.explanation: Both release energy overall, but rusting proceeds so slowly that the heat dissipates as fast as it is produced, so no flame or glow is seen.

options.text: rusting releases its energy far more slowly
rusting releases no energy at all
options.why: Rusting is exothermic; iron filings in hand-warmers work on exactly this reaction.

options.text: rusting is not really an oxidation
options.why: Rust is hydrated iron(III) oxide, so oxygen is definitely added to the iron.

options.text: magnesium does not need oxygen to burn
options.why: Burning in air is combination with oxygen; without it the ribbon would not burn.

2723.stem: Two students dissolve the same mass of a white solid in water. One tube warms, the other cools. The most reasonable inference is that
2723.explanation: The same solid cannot be both exothermic and endothermic on dissolving, so the two white solids must be different substances.

options.text: the two white solids are different substances
one student measured the mass incorrectly
options.why: Mass affects how much the temperature changes, never its direction.

options.text: the water was at different temperatures
options.why: The starting temperature does not reverse whether heat is absorbed or released.
Contamination might disturb a result slightly but would not reverse the energy change.

2723.stem: Evaporating sea water leaves salt, while burning wood leaves ash. Both leave a solid residue, yet only one is a chemical change. The decisive difference is that
2723.explanation: The salt is chemically identical to what was dissolved and can be redissolved, whereas ash is a set of new substances that cannot be turned back into wood.

options.text: the salt is the original substance while the ash is not
one residue is white and the other is grey
options.why: Colour of the residue is a property, not a test for chemical change.

options.text: one process needs heat and the other does not
options.why: Both processes involve heating, so heat cannot be the deciding factor.

options.text: one leaves more residue than the other
options.why: The quantity of residue says nothing about whether new substances formed.

2723.stem: A reaction produces a gas, but when the experiment is repeated in a sealed flask on a balance the total mass does not change. This shows that
2723.explanation: The gas is still inside the sealed flask, so no matter has left the system and the law of conservation of mass holds.

options.text: the gas stayed inside the flask

options.why: The open experiment clearly produced gas; sealing the flask only stops it escaping.
The constant mass is exactly what conservation of mass predicts, so the balance is behaving correctly.

options.text: gases do not have any mass
options.why: Gases do have mass, which is why an open flask loses weight as the gas escapes.

2723.stem: Assertion: A change in colour always proves a chemical reaction. Reason: Chemical reactions form new substances with new properties. Which is correct?
2723.explanation: The reason is true, but the assertion is too strong: adding a dye or mixing paints changes colour without forming any new substance.

options.text: The reason is true but the assertion is too strong
Both are true and the reason explains the assertion
options.why: Accepts the word 'always'; a counter-example such as mixing paints defeats it.
The reason is a correct statement of what a chemical reaction does.

options.text: The assertion is true but the reason is false
options.why: Inverts which statement fails; forming new substances is exactly what defines a reaction.

2723.stem: Which experimental design would BEST distinguish a physical change from a chemical change?
2723.explanation: Attempting to recover the starting materials unchanged tests the defining property directly: a physical change is reversible to the original substance, a chemical change is not.

options.text: Try to recover the starting materials unchanged
Measure how long the change takes
options.why: Speed varies enormously within both kinds of change and separates neither.

options.text: Check whether the sample changed colour
options.why: Colour change is suggestive but can also occur without new substances forming.

options.text: Weigh the sample before the change only
options.why: A single measurement gives nothing to compare against.

2723.stem: A gas is evolved when a substance is warmed and the residue weighs less than the original. A student says this disproves conservation of mass. The student is
2723.explanation: Mass appears lost only because the gas escaped from the open container; counting the gas restores the balance exactly.

options.text: wrong, because the escaped gas was not weighed

options.why: Considers only what remained in the vessel and ignores what left it.
Heating supplies energy to rearrange atoms; it never destroys them.

options.text: wrong, because the balance reads only solids
options.why: Reaches the right verdict by inventing a limitation the balance does not have.

2723.stem: Copper carbonate is heated and turns black. A student concludes it has burnt. The most accurate criticism is that
2723.explanation: Burning means combining with oxygen, but here the compound has broken down into copper oxide and carbon dioxide, which is decomposition, not combustion.

options.text: the substance decomposed rather than combined with oxygen
black colour cannot indicate a reaction
options.why: The colour change is genuine evidence of change; the error is in naming the type.
Carbon dioxide is released and a new solid forms, so a reaction certainly occurred.
It is heated routinely; thermal decomposition is exactly what it undergoes.

2723.stem: In which case would you need MORE than one observation before safely concluding a chemical reaction had occurred?
2723.explanation: Bubbles alone can also come from dissolved air escaping or from boiling, so a further sign is needed before concluding a reaction occurred.

options.text: Bubbles appearing in a warmed liquid
A new insoluble solid settling from two solutions
options.why: A precipitate cannot arise without a new substance being formed.

options.text: A permanent smell of a new substance
options.why: A persistent new smell means a new compound is present.

options.text: A metal turning into a flaky oxide
options.why: The flaky oxide is a new compound with completely different properties.

2723.stem: Sodium hydroxide solution is added to hydrochloric acid and the mixture warms, yet stays colourless with no gas or solid. The strongest evidence of reaction is
2723.explanation: With no visible sign available, the released heat is the evidence; neutralisation is exothermic even though nothing can be seen.

options.why: Remaining clear is the absence of a sign, not the presence of one.
Volumes add in any mixing, reaction or not.
Describes the starting materials rather than any change.

2723.stem: Two reactions give the same gas. One turns lime water milky and the other does not, though both bubble equally. The best conclusion is that
2723.explanation: The lime water test identifies carbon dioxide specifically, so the two gases must be different despite looking identical while bubbling.

options.text: the two gases are different substances

options.why: Both were observed to bubble equally, so gas was produced in both.

options.text: the lime water was too dilute in one case
options.why: Possible in principle, but blaming the reagent before accepting the simplest explanation is poor reasoning.

options.text: bubbling proves the gases are identical
options.why: Bubbling shows only that a gas is present, never which gas it is.

2723.stem: A teacher says: 'Every chemical reaction shows at least one of the five indications.' The most careful response is that
2723.explanation: Some reactions show no visible sign at all, and a temperature change may be too small to feel, so the statement holds only if measurement is sensitive enough.

options.text: it holds only if the change can be measured sensitively enough
it is always true without qualification
options.why: Overlooks reactions whose energy change is too small to detect by hand.
Most reactions studied at this level do show at least one clear indication.

options.text: it applies only to reactions in solution
options.why: The indications apply equally to reactions of solids and gases.
